nameStory: The Black Slug gets its straightforward name from its most common color form - a deep, rich black that makes it look like a miniature piece of dark rubber crawling across the forest floor. However, this slug is a bit of a shape-shifter and can actually range from jet black to brown, orange, or even reddish, so the name only tells part of the story!
description: The Black Slug is a large, shell-less mollusk that glides along on a trail of slime, much like its snail cousins but without the spiral house on its back. These hefty gastropods can grow quite large - up to 6 inches long when fully extended - making them one of the biggest slugs you'll encounter in New England. They have a smooth, rounded back (hence their family name 'roundback slugs') and two pairs of tentacles on their head, with the longer upper pair carrying their eyes.

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Large and robust with a distinctly rounded, arched back that feels firm and muscular when gently touched (use a stick, not your finger!). When contracted, they form a tight, dome-like hump.

idTips.label: Slime Trail
idTips.description: Leaves behind a thick, clear to slightly milky mucus trail that feels sticky and stretchy between your fingers and may have a faintly bitter or metallic taste if accidentally encountered.

idTips.label: Color Variation
idTips.description: Despite the name, can be black, dark brown, reddish-brown, orange, or even yellowish. The body often has a subtle sheen when moist, like wet leather.

idTips.label: Breathing Pore
idTips.description: Look for a round breathing hole (pneumostome) on the right side of the body, about one-third back from the head. It opens and closes rhythmically, especially visible when the slug is active.

idTips.label: Head Tentacles
idTips.description: Four retractable tentacles - two long upper ones with black eye spots at the tips, and two shorter lower ones used for smell and taste. They can completely withdraw them when startled.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Skin appears smooth and glistening when moist, but feels slightly granular or pebbly to the touch, especially on the upper mantle area behind the head.

habitat: Black Slugs thrive in moist, shaded areas throughout New England's forests, gardens, and parks, particularly favoring rich, organic soil under fallen logs, leaf litter, and mulched garden beds. You'll often find them in deciduous and mixed forests where the soil stays consistently damp, as well as around compost piles, underneath deck boards, and in well-watered flower gardens.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and spring rains provide ideal moisture conditions. Look for them emerging from winter hiding spots under logs and stones, often leaving obvious slime trails on sidewalks after rain.
seasonality.summer: Active mainly during cooler, humid nights and early mornings, retreating to shady, moist hideouts during hot, dry days. Best found by checking under garden mulch or boards after watering.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they feed heavily before winter, often seen crossing paths and driveways on damp autumn nights. This is prime time for slug watching as they're less secretive about daytime activity.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under logs, stones, or in soil crevices in a dormant state. Occasionally emerge during warm winter thaws, but generally inactive until spring temperatures return.

funFact: Black Slugs are hermaphrodites that perform an elaborate aerial mating dance, hanging from a string of mucus while intertwined together - sometimes for hours - before exchanging sperm packets in mid-air!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other large Arion slugs, especially the Western Dusky Slug, but Black Slugs are generally larger and more robust with that characteristic rounded, muscular back. Memory trick: 'Black and brawny' - even when they're not black in color, they're always the beefiest slug around.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'Black' Slug, remember that color is actually the least reliable way to identify this species since they come in many colors. This European native is considered invasive in New England, having hitchhiked here in soil and plant shipments, and can become a garden pest by munching on vegetables and flowers.
compareHints: Black Slugs are the largest and most robust of the Arion genus in New England, with that distinctive rounded back that sets them apart from their smaller, more elongated relatives like the Western Dusky Slug or Garden Arion. While other Arion species tend to be more consistently colored and smaller, Black Slugs are the hefty variable ones - think of them as the 'linebacker' of the slug world compared to their more slender cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Arion slugs, the Western Dusky Slug is one of the smallest and plainest-looking members of its genus.
Among its Arion relatives, the hedgehog slug is most distinctive for its defensive curling behavior - the Black Slug and Garden Arion don't ball up nearly as dramatically.
Garden Arions are smaller and more compact than their relatives like the Black Slug, which can grow much larger and stays more elongated when disturbed.
Within the Arion genus, the Northern Dusky Slug is much smaller and more subdued in color compared to the large, jet-black Black Slug or the distinctively marked Orange-banded Arion.

Among its Arion relatives in New England, the Orange-banded Arion is the only one with prominent orange side bands - the Black Slug is uniformly dark, the Garden Arion is typically smaller and grayer, and the Dusky Slugs lack any bright coloration.

Among New England's Arion slugs, the Darkface Arion is most easily distinguished by its characteristic dark facial markings, while the Garden Arion tends to be more uniformly colored and the Black Slug is typically much larger and darker overall.
